title: Nvidia's Groq 3 LPX inference chip hits full production at 3,400 tokens/sec
subtitle: The dedicated inference silicon from Nvidia's $20B Groq acqui-hire slots into Vera Rubin racks, with Nebius as launch customer.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Nvidia said on August 24 that its Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator has entered full production and is shipping into Vera Rubin NVL72 racks at up to 256 LPX units per rack. In a reference configuration running the open-weight Gemma 4 31B model at a 100,000-token context window, the combined system generated 3,400 output tokens per second — Nvidia's fastest published inference figure to date. The company claims the setup delivers roughly four times the responsiveness of the nearest alternative platform for latency-sensitive agent workloads. Nebius Group signed on as the first named customer.

The interesting thing about Groq 3 LPX is that it is not a general-purpose GPU. It is dedicated inference silicon — the product of the $20 billion acqui-hire that pulled Groq's LPU team inside Nvidia last year — and its whole reason for existing is to make agent loops feel instantaneous. Training still runs on Rubin GPUs; LPX takes the finished model and streams tokens back to the caller as fast as the memory bandwidth allows. That specialization matters because agentic workloads spend most of their wall-clock time in the inference step, not the reasoning step, and shaving latency there compounds across every tool call an agent makes.

This is the clearest sign yet that the AI hardware market is splitting into two distinct workloads with different economics: training chips optimized for FLOPS and memory capacity, and inference chips optimized for tokens per second per watt. AMD's MI355X, AWS Trainium 3, Google TPU v6, and now Nvidia's own LPX line are all pushing that direction. For a data center buyer, that means the old habit of buying one class of GPU and hoping it stays good for both jobs is over — the next generation of racks will be mixed by design.

For learners: when you read a benchmark like '3,400 tokens per second,' translate it into user experience before you compare specs. That's roughly 50 pages of English text every minute — fast enough that an agent making 10 tool calls in a row completes in the time a slower system takes to answer one. Latency is the feature that people actually feel; throughput per dollar is what determines whether a startup can afford to serve them. Getting fluent in that translation is more useful than memorizing chip names.
